title: Phenylketonuria
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: A rare autosomal recessive inborn error of phenylalanine metabolism. Untreated leads to neurocognitive decline; early diet controls phenylalanine, preventing damage.

sections.p: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. The excess phenylalanine and its toxic metabolites damage the developing brain.
b: Early detection by newborn screening is essential

sections.p: PAH uses tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor to hydroxylate phenylalanine. In PKU, PAH activity is <10% of normal, so phenylalanine accumulates.
b: BH4 can be supplemented in some patients

sections.p: PAH is regulated by phenylalanine itself (feedback inhibition) and by BH4 availability. In low-resource settings, BH4 testing is rarely available.
b: Dietary restriction of phenylalanine is the mainstay

sections.p: High plasma phenylalanine (>360 µmol/L) interferes with myelin synthesis and neurotransmitter production, causing intellectual disability, seizures, and behavioral problems.
b: Severity graded by phenylalanine levels: mild PKU 360–600 µmol/L, classic PKU >600 µmol/L

t.b: Positive in classic PKU; confirms diagnosis when screening positive

sections.p: In East Africa, PKU is often missed because newborn screening is limited. Children may present with developmental delay, eczema, and a musty odor. Early dietary therapy prevents irreversible damage.
b: Look for developmental regression after 12 months

t.b: Detects elevated phenylalanine; if unavailable, use clinical suspicion and plasma phenylalanine
Reduces plasma levels; monitor growth and neurodevelopment

sections.p: Treat the cause (diet) and monitor. Use a low-protein formula and phenylalanine-free amino acid mix. Monitor plasma phenylalanine every 3–6 months. In severe cases, BH4 supplementation may be tried if available.
b: Avoid high-protein foods: meat, dairy, nuts

t.b: Provides essential amino acids without phenylalanine; essential for growth
Used in patients with residual PAH activity; reduces phenylalanine levels

sections.p: Other inborn errors of metabolism can mimic PKU symptoms. Distinguish by specific biochemical markers.
b: Maple syrup urine disease – sweet urine odor, ketotic hypoglycaemia

t.b: Positive for branched-chain ketoacids in MSUD; negative in PKU

sections.p: In malnutrition, plasma phenylalanine may be falsely low. In patients on protein-restricted diets, levels may appear normal but still neurotoxic.
b: Check dietary intake when interpreting phenylalanine levels

sections.p: Remember the classic triad: developmental delay, eczema, musty odor. Newborn screening is the only way to prevent cognitive loss. In low-resource settings, a high plasma phenylalanine (>600 µmol/L) on a random blood spot is diagnostic.
b: Ask about family history of PKU

sections.p: Urgent referral if a child shows rapid regression, seizures, or severe eczema with failure to thrive.
b: Seizures, severe developmental delay, or failure to thrive

faq.q: What is the first test if newborn screening is unavailable?
faq.a: A random plasma phenylalanine measurement; >360 µmol/L suggests PKU.

faq.q: Can a child with PKU live a normal life?
faq.a: With strict diet and monitoring, normal growth and mild intellectual function are achievable.

faq.q: Why is a musty odor seen in PKU?
faq.a: Accumulation of phenylacetate gives a phenylketone smell similar to old socks.

exam: A 10‑month‑old boy with developmental delay and eczema – what is the most likely diagnosis? — PKU; look for musty odor and high phenylalanine.
A child with high phenylalanine but normal growth – what should you suspect? — Possible dietary non‑compliance or malabsorption.
You have a patient with classic PKU; which drug can reduce phenylalanine levels? — Sapropterin (BH4) in patients with residual PAH activity.
During a ward round you notice a child with seizures and a sweet urine odor – what is the differential? — Maple syrup urine disease vs. PKU; check urine organic acids.
A mother reports her child’s growth is poor despite a low‑protein diet – what is the next step? — Re‑measure plasma phenylalanine and assess dietary intake.
You are in a rural clinic with no newborn screening – what is the most cost‑effective way to detect PKU? — Measure plasma phenylalanine in symptomatic infants.
